triage.name: Vaginitis
triage.reason: Very common cause of vaginal discharge and itching; diagnosis reachable by history, exam and wet mount/pH testing, with classic distinguishing features among causes.

demographics: Most common in women of reproductive age
Bacterial vaginosis is the most common vaginal infection in women ages 15–44
Can occur in postmenopausal women, especially with estrogen deficiency or atrophic changes

risk_factors.text: Douching or use of vaginal sprays or scented products
New or multiple sexual partners, or unprotected sex
Use of systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants
Use of spermicides or a new soap, detergent, or fabric softener
Tight, non-breathable clothing or synthetic underwear

social_history: Sexual activity, including new or multiple partners
Use of scented feminine hygiene products
exposures: Vaginal sprays, douches, spermicides, soaps, detergents, or fabric softeners

chief_complaints.text: I have vaginal discharge that won't go away
My vagina and vulva itch and burn
There is a bad smell down there

hpi.duration: Days to weeks; often recurrent or persistent
hpi.progression: Discharge and irritation develop over several days; symptoms may fluctuate with menstrual cycle or after intercourse
hpi.quality: Discharge may be thin and gray, thick and white like cottage cheese, or gray-green; itching and burning are common
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; can be severe with marked itching or soreness
hpi.timing: Persistent; may worsen after intercourse or at certain points in the menstrual cycle

associated_symptoms.text: Abnormal vaginal discharge (color, amount, or odor change)
Vaginal or vulvar burning or soreness
Fishy or foul odor, especially after sex
Redness or swelling of the vulva

pertinent_negatives: Heavy vaginal bleeding or bleeding between periods

atypical.how_it_differs: Vaginitis may be asymptomatic or symptoms may be attributed to normal pregnancy changes; bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis increase risk of preterm labor and preterm birth.
Postmenopausal women may have atrophic vaginitis with dryness, burning, and dyspareunia rather than discharge; symptoms overlap with other causes.
Poorly controlled diabetes predisposes to recurrent yeast infections; symptoms may be more severe and persistent.
May have more severe or atypical symptoms, including extensive candidiasis or mixed infections.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; normal general appearance
general.moderate: Mild discomfort or restlessness from itching or burning; otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Visibly uncomfortable, guarding the perineum, reluctant to sit still
general.critical: Not typical for uncomplicated vaginitis; if toxic-appearing, consider another diagnosis such as pelvic inflammatory disease or systemic infection

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vulva and perineum with good lighting
findings.finding: Erythema and edema of the vulva and vaginal introitus

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vaginal vault and note discharge character, color, and amount
findings.finding: Abnormal vaginal discharge (thin gray, thick white cottage-cheese, or gray-green)

findings.maneuver: Assess discharge odor, including after adding potassium hydroxide (whiff test)
findings.finding: Fishy or foul odor, often accentuated by KOH

findings.maneuver: Test vaginal fluid pH with pH paper
findings.finding: pH greater than 4.5 (suggests bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis)

findings.maneuver: Perform bimanual exam and move the cervix
Bimanual exam to assess uterine size, mobility, and adnexa
findings.finding: Normal-sized, mobile, non-tender uterus and no adnexal masses

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vulva, vagina, and cervix for ulcers or vesicles
findings.finding: No genital ulcers, vesicles, or erosions

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and assess for systemic signs
Palpate the abdomen for tenderness, guarding, or masses
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding or rebound

decision_points: Pregnancy test before treatment or imaging in anyone who could be pregnant
Vaginal pH above 4.5 points to bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis; normal pH points to candidiasis
Wet mount showing clue cells, motile trichomonads, or yeast directs therapy; if nondiagnostic, send NAAT for Trichomonas
Cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, fever, or systemic illness should redirect the workup toward pelvic inflammatory disease
Recurrent or refractory candidiasis should prompt testing for diabetes and consideration of non-albicans Candida

criteria.name: Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis
criteria.summary: Diagnosis requires at least three of: thin homogeneous gray-white discharge, vaginal pH above 4.5, a positive whiff test (fishy amine odor after KOH), and clue cells on saline wet mount.
items: Clue cells on saline wet mount

criteria.name: Nugent score for bacterial vaginosis
criteria.summary: A Gram stain scoring system based on the relative amounts of Lactobacillus morphotypes, Gardnerella/Bacteroides morphotypes, and curved gram-variable rods; higher scores indicate bacterial vaginosis.

differential.name: Bacterial vaginosis
differential.why_considered: Most common cause of vaginal discharge in reproductive-age women; thin gray discharge with fishy odor

history: Recent antibiotics, douching, IUD, or new sexual partner
exam: Thin homogeneous gray discharge coating the vaginal walls
Positive whiff test (fishy amine odor after KOH)
Vulva and vagina usually not markedly inflamed
labs: Clue cells on saline wet mount

differential.name: Vulvovaginal candidiasis
differential.why_considered: Common cause of intense vulvar itching with thick white discharge

history: Recent antibiotics, pregnancy, diabetes, or corticosteroid use
exam: Vulvar and vaginal erythema and edema
labs: Budding yeast and pseudohyphae on KOH wet mount

differential.name: Trichomoniasis
differential.why_considered: Sexually transmitted infection causing discharge, itching, and dysuria

exam: Strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages) in some cases
labs: Motile trichomonads on saline wet mount

differential.name: Atrophic vaginitis
differential.why_considered: Vaginal dryness, burning, and dyspareunia in postmenopausal or estrogen-deficient women

history: Gradual onset of vaginal dryness and burning
labs: Normal wet mount without clue cells, trichomonads, or yeast

differential.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal pain, discharge, and dyspareunia in a sexually active woman
differential.trigger: Pelvic or lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, or fever

labs: Positive NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae
imaging: Thickened, fluid-filled fallopian tube or tubo-ovarian complex on pelvic ultrasound

differential.name: Genital herpes simplex virus infection
differential.why_considered: Vulvar pain, burning, and dysuria that can be mistaken for vaginitis

exam: Vesicles, ulcers, or erosions on vulva, vagina, or cervix
labs: Positive NAAT or PCR for herpes simplex virus from lesion swab
Negative wet mount for clue cells, trichomonads, or yeast

differential.name: Vaginal cancer
differential.why_considered: Persistent vaginal discharge or bleeding that does not respond to treatment for common vaginitis
differential.trigger: Persistent or bloody discharge, postcoital bleeding, or a visible vaginal lesion that fails to improve with standard therapy

history: Symptoms not responding to treatment for vaginitis
History of HPV or cervical cancer
exam: Visible ulcerated or exophytic vaginal lesion
imaging: Pelvic MRI or CT showing vaginal mass and extent of disease

severity.mild: Mild discharge or itching without significant discomfort; normal daily activities unaffected; no fever or pelvic pain
severity.moderate: Persistent discharge, itching, burning, or odor causing bother and some interference with daily activities; no systemic symptoms
severity.severe: Marked vulvar and vaginal inflammation with intense itching, burning, dysuria, or dyspareunia; may have extensive candidiasis or recurrent symptoms; no systemic toxicity
severity.critical: Not typical for uncomplicated vaginitis; if toxic-appearing with fever, hypotension, or severe pelvic pain, consider pelvic inflammatory disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, or sepsis

red_flags.meaning: Suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or another systemic infection rather than uncomplicated vaginitis
Suggests pelvic inflammatory disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, or another pelvic process

red_flags.finding: Cervical motion tenderness or adnexal tenderness or mass
red_flags.meaning: Suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or tubo-ovarian abscess; requires prompt evaluation and treatment

red_flags.finding: Heavy vaginal bleeding or bleeding between periods
red_flags.meaning: Requires evaluation for malignancy, pregnancy complications, or other bleeding source
Suggests herpes simplex virus or another ulcerative genital condition

red_flags.finding: Persistent or bloody discharge not responding to treatment
red_flags.meaning: Suggests vaginal cancer or another malignancy; requires biopsy
Changes treatment choices and raises risk of preterm labor with bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis

complications.name: Increased risk of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections
clues: Ongoing sexual activity without barrier protection

complications.name: Preterm labor and preterm birth
clues: Pregnancy with bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis

special_populations.differences: Bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis increase the risk of preterm labor and preterm birth; treatment is recommended. Symptoms may be attributed to normal pregnancy changes, and treatment choices must be pregnancy-safe.
Postmenopausal women may have atrophic vaginitis with dryness, burning, and dyspareunia rather than discharge; symptoms overlap with other causes and may respond to estrogen cream.
Poorly controlled diabetes predisposes to recurrent yeast infections; symptoms may be more severe and persistent, and glycemic control is part of management.
May have more severe or atypical symptoms, including extensive candidiasis or mixed infections, and may require longer or alternative treatment.

key_questions.question: What does the discharge look like — color, thickness, and amount?
key_questions.looking_for: Thin gray-white suggests bacterial vaginosis; thick white cottage-cheese suggests candidiasis; frothy gray-green suggests trichomoniasis

key_questions.question: Is there an odor, and is it worse after sex?
key_questions.looking_for: Fishy amine odor worse after intercourse points to bacterial vaginosis; absent odor favors candidiasis

key_questions.question: How bad is the itching?
key_questions.looking_for: Intense vulvar itching favors candidiasis; minimal itching favors bacterial vaginosis

key_questions.question: When did the symptoms start and how have they changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days; chronic or recurrent symptoms suggest atrophic vaginitis, recurrent candidiasis, or a noninfectious cause

key_questions.question: Do you have pain or burning with urination?
key_questions.looking_for: External dysuria from inflamed vulvar tissue; trichomoniasis commonly causes dysuria

key_questions.question: Is sex painful?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspareunia, common with candidiasis, trichomoniasis, and atrophic vaginitis

key_questions.question: Have you taken antibiotics recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotics predispose to both bacterial vaginosis and candidiasis

key_questions.question: Do you use corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, or hormonal medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Corticosteroids and immunosuppression predispose to candidiasis; hormonal status matters for atrophic changes

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, or is your blood sugar poorly controlled?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes, especially uncontrolled, predisposes to recurrent yeast infections

key_questions.question: Are you pregnant, or could you be? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes treatment choices and raises the risk of preterm labor with bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis

key_questions.question: Are you sexually active, and do you have a new or multiple partners?
key_questions.looking_for: New or multiple partners raises concern for trichomoniasis and coexisting sexually transmitted infections

key_questions.question: Do you douche or use vaginal sprays, scented soaps, spermicides, or new detergents?
key_questions.looking_for: Irritant or allergic vaginitis and a strong risk factor for bacterial vaginosis

key_questions.question: Do you have any fever, pelvic pain, or bleeding between periods?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever, pelvic pain, or abnormal bleeding suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or malignancy rather than uncomplicated vaginitis

key_questions.question: Have you had genital sores or blisters?
key_questions.looking_for: Ulcerative lesions suggest herpes simplex virus rather than vaginitis

key_questions.question: Have you had these symptoms before, and did treatment help?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent or treatment-refractory symptoms suggest diabetes, non-albicans Candida, or another diagnosis

reasoning_points: Abnormal vaginal discharge with itching, burning, or odor in a reproductive-age woman
Discharge character narrows the cause: thin gray-white with fishy odor suggests bacterial vaginosis, thick white cottage-cheese suggests candidiasis, frothy gray-green suggests trichomoniasis
Vaginal pH above 4.5 points to bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis; normal pH points to candidiasis
Saline wet mount findings of clue cells, motile trichomonads, or budding yeast and pseudohyphae direct therapy
Positive whiff test with KOH supports bacterial vaginosis
Pregnancy excluded before treatment and imaging decisions
Absence of fever, pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, and adnexal tenderness argues against pelvic inflammatory disease
Recurrent or refractory candidiasis should prompt testing for diabetes and consideration of non-albicans Candida

easy: Reproductive-age woman with classic discharge and itching
Discharge character matches one cause exactly
Vaginal pH and wet mount confirm the diagnosis
No fever, pelvic pain, or systemic symptoms
medium: Mixed or overlapping symptoms that do not fit one cause cleanly
Postmenopausal woman with dryness, burning, and dyspareunia suggesting atrophic vaginitis
Recurrent yeast infections prompting evaluation for diabetes
Dysuria that could be mistaken for a urinary tract infection
hard: Persistent or bloody discharge not responding to treatment, raising concern for vaginal cancer
Pregnant patient where treatment choices and preterm risk must be weighed
Immunocompromised patient with extensive or atypical candidiasis
Symptoms that overlap with pelvic inflammatory disease or herpes simplex virus
